History and Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
42-year-old woman with sudden-onset continuous spinning vertigo, tinnitus, and nausea for ≈2 hours, likely acute vestibular neuritis / viral labyrinthitis; empiric anti-vertigo medication prescribed and in-person evaluation arranged.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Sudden dizziness described as “room spinning,” associated ear buzzing and nausea.  
• Onset & course: Began abruptly ≈2 h prior while making breakfast; persistent since. Similar but much shorter episode (5–10 min) 1 month ago that resolved spontaneously.  
• Aggravating/relieving factors: None identified; not positional.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Tinnitus (“ears buzzing”).  
  – Unsteady gait; veers when walking but no limb weakness.  
  – No vomiting (feels very sick), no headache, no visual changes.  
  – No ear pain, discharge, muffled hearing, fever, cough, or recent viral illness.  
• Review of systems (pertinent negatives stated): no focal neurologic deficits, no limb weakness, no prior similar prolonged episodes.

Past Medical History:
• Premature ovarian failure – on hormone-replacement therapy (HRT).  
• No other chronic illnesses or previous surgeries mentioned.

Medications:
• Hormone-replacement therapy – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• New prescription (anti-vertigo agent; specific drug name not captured in transcript) – “1 tablet three times daily for 10 days.”

Allergies:
• Denies drug allergies.

Social History:
• Lives with husband; no additional social, smoking, alcohol, or substance history provided.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
(Video only – no vitals documented)  
• General: Appears dizzy but alert and oriented.  
• Neurologic: Patient reports full strength in arms/legs; ambulates with unsteadiness due to vertigo.  
• Ear: Reports tinnitus; no pain or discharge reported.  
(Full exam deferred to in-person visit.)

Investigations:
• None performed during tele-visit. Plan for otoscopic exam, blood pressure check, and gait assessment at upcoming appointment.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Acute vestibular syndrome, most consistent with vestibular neuritis / viral labyrinthitis:  
  • Empiric anti-vertigo medication prescribed (1 tablet TID ×10 days; medication name not documented).  
  • Arrange face-to-face evaluation with clinic physician for otoscopic exam, neurologic exam, and vitals.  
  • Safety-net advice: Seek emergency care (A&E) if new limb weakness, sudden severe headache, or persistent vomiting develops.  

Issue 2 – Rule out central causes of vertigo (e.g., posterior-circulation stroke/TIA):  
  • Will assess neurologic status in person; consider urgent imaging if focal deficits appear.  
  • Patient educated on red-flag symptoms as above.

General advice:  
  • May take medication with or without food.  
  • Contact support to book appointment; follow-up expected within next few days.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Vestibular neuritis / viral labyrinthitis – High likelihood: acute continuous vertigo, tinnitus, gait unsteadiness, no focal deficits.  
2. Ménière’s disease – Moderate likelihood: recurrent vertigo with tinnitus; absence of fluctuating hearing loss makes less likely.  
3. Posterior-circulation (cerebellar) stroke/TIA – Low-moderate likelihood: acute vertigo with imbalance; no vascular risk factors or focal neuro signs, but cannot be excluded without exam.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Full medication list (only HRT noted), dosage details for new prescription, detailed allergy review, social history (smoking/alcohol), complete neurologic and ear examination, vital signs.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; one instance where drug name not captured/inaudible.
